narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies eclipsing binary stars in TESS satellite data and checks them for false signals caused by instrument artifacts or nearby stars. The pipeline begins by sampling target stars and extracting their light curves, then applies statistical tests to identify dips in brightness consistent with eclipses. Candidates are cross-matched against six existing variable-star catalogs to flag known objects, then undergo an automated pixel-level check to confirm the dimming comes from the target star itself rather than contamination. The result is a list of candidates that passed this vetting funnel. We also train a machine learning model to score each candidate as a second opinion, showing how the current automated workflow compares to a human-like classifier. So far, we have vetted 18,522 stars across 2.1% of the TESS survey area, confirming 266 candidates as on-target eclipsing binaries. While these candidates represent genuine eclipsing systems found by TESS, follow-up observations by other researchers remain the path to full scientific characterization.

faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary star?
faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other in such a way that, from Earth's viewpoint, one star periodically passes in front of the other. Each time this happens, we see a dip in the total brightness of the system. By studying these eclipse patterns in detail, astronomers can learn about the sizes, masses, and orbits of distant stars.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a 'candidate' and a 'confirmed' result on this site?
faqs.answer: A candidate is any star that passed our statistical vetting and novelty checks but has not yet been examined at pixel resolution. 'Confirmed' on this site means the candidate survived our automated pixel-level check, which examines whether the eclipse signal comes from the target star itself or from a nearby star contaminating the signal. Confirmation here is specific to this pipeline and does not imply scientific verification by independent observers.

faqs.question: What is the machine learning score and what does it do?
faqs.answer: We train a machine learning model (gradient boosting) on our vetted candidates to estimate how likely each candidate is to be a real eclipsing binary. This score serves as a second opinion, showing how well an automated statistical approach compares to the current rule-based pipeline. The ML score itself does not gate, filter, or decide which candidates are checked - that decision remains based on our baseline rules. It is provided as a reference metric only.

faqs.question: How does the pixel-level check work?
faqs.answer: The pixel-level check is a fully automated test that examines whether the dimming in the light curve originates from the target star or from a nearby star in the same field of view. The algorithm looks at the spatial distribution of photons across pixels in the TESS image. If the eclipse signal correlates with the target star's centroid, it passes; if it correlates with a nearby star, it is flagged as contaminated. This entire process runs automatically without human intervention.

faqs.question: What if the eclipse period looks like it could be aliased?
faqs.answer: We perform a period-alias check by comparing the depths of odd-numbered eclipses to even-numbered eclipses in the light curve. If these depths differ significantly, it suggests we may be seeing every other eclipse and the true period is twice what we measured. This check flags such cases as caveats on individual candidate pages, alerting users that the reported period may need further scrutiny.

faqs.question: Can I verify a result myself by looking at the light curve?
faqs.answer: Yes. Every candidate has a light curve plot and detailed vetting information on its page. You can examine the eclipse pattern, see which catalogs were checked, review the pixel-level check results, and read any period-alias or other caveats. You can make your own assessment, though confirming these candidates through independent observations requires access to follow-up telescopes.

faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it is listed on this site?
faqs.answer: Being listed on Star Vetter represents the end of this automated pipeline's work. The candidates are now public, and individual researchers may choose to perform follow-up observations using ground-based telescopes, spectroscopy, or other methods to characterize them further. This site itself does not carry out, coordinate, or track any such follow-up efforts.
